abstract.p: Este artículo analiza un conjunto contemporáneo recuperado de un pozo excavado en la roca dentro del Complejo Prehistórico de Ħal Tarxien, Malta. Reabierto en 2010 y abierto hasta 2024, el rasgo acumuló monedas y diversos objetos modernos depositados tanto de forma intencional como no intencional. El conjunto fue retirado, documentado y clasificado de manera sistemática mediante un marco que distingue entre deposición significativa, comportamiento colectivo, pérdida accidental y material introducido externamente. El análisis de 941 monedas no euro agrupadas en 46 categorías por país revela diversidad geográfica. La comparación con los registros de visitantes plantea posibles diferencias en las prácticas de deposición, aunque los distintos periodos de registro, la declaración voluntaria de procedencia y el origen incierto de los depositantes limitan su interpretación. Los demás objetos, incluidos cristales, elementos devocionales y fichas de valor personal, sugieren que algunos visitantes interpretan el entorno prehistórico como un espacio para la práctica espiritual, la conmemoración y la construcción de identidad, mientras que otros objetos reflejan pérdidas cotidianas y procesos tafonómicos del sitio. El estudio sostiene que los depósitos contemporáneos constituyen evidencia de procesos continuos de patrimonialización y expone las implicaciones prácticas y éticas para la conservación y la gestión del sitio.

trans-abstract.p: This paper analyses a contemporary assemblage recovered from a rock-cut pit within the Ħal Tarxien Prehistoric Complex, Malta. Reopened in 2010 and open until 2024, the feature accumulated coins and a diverse range of modern objects deposited both intentionally and unintentionally. The assemblage was systematically removed, documented and classified using a framework distinguishing meaningful deposition, collective behaviour, accidental loss and externally introduced material. Analysis of 941 non-euro coins grouped into 46 country categories reveals geographical diversity. Comparison with visitor records raises the possibility of variation in depositional engagement, although different recording periods, voluntary reporting and uncertain depositor origins limit interpretation. Non-coin objects, including crystals, devotional items and personally significant tokens, suggest that some visitors interpret the prehistoric setting as a locus for spiritual practice, commemoration and identity work, while other items reflect mundane loss and site taphonomy. The study argues that contemporary deposits constitute evidence for ongoing heritage-making and outlines the practical and ethical implications for conservation and site management.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Archaeological sites do not cease to accumulate material once their original periods of use come to an end. Across the world, prehistoric monuments and historic places continue to attract the intentional deposition of coins, tokens, personal items and other objects left by visitors seeking luck, healing, commemoration, spiritual connection, or other forms of meaningful engagement (Äikäs & Ahola, 2020; Blain & Wallis, 2004; Finn, 1997; Houlbrook, 2015; Jonuks & Äikäs, 2019). Such practices have been documented at a wide range of sites, from prehistoric (Blain & Wallis, 2004) to sacred natural places (Jonuks & Äikäs, 2019), demonstrating that heritage landscapes remain socially and materially active in the present. Rather than representing isolated or aberrant behaviour, these deposits form part of broader contemporary practices through which people engage with the past, negotiate belief, and inscribe personal meaning onto ancient places.

Scholarly research has shown that modern deposits are frequently left intentionally and with symbolic purpose, even when their meanings diverge from dominant archaeological interpretations of the sites themselves. A study of Chaco Canyon demonstrated how crystals, shells, and ritual objects deposited by visitors function as modern votive offerings, raising questions as to whether such materials should be dismissed as “junk” or recognised as evidence of ongoing cultural use and meaning-making (Finn, 1997). A similar study of contemporary coin deposition has shown that the act of leaving a coin, whether in a fountain, well or at an archaeological monument, often constitutes a ritualised practice motivated by wishing, luck, remembrance or participation in a shared tradition rather than by economic value (Houlbrook, 2015). These studies emphasise that intentional contemporary deposits are not random intrusions but patterned behaviours embedded within wider social and cultural frameworks. Despite this growing body of work, contemporary deposits at archaeological sites are still commonly treated primarily as conservation problems rather than as material deserving respect and analytical attention. Objects deposited by visitors are routinely removed during site maintenance, often without systematic documentation, classification or interpretation and it has been noted that such materials are frequently labelled as “ritual litter” (Blain & Wallis, 2004: 241), a term that reflects heritage management concerns but risks obscuring the social, spiritual and identity-based motivations underpinning these practices. As a consequence, valuable material evidence for contemporary engagements with the past is often lost, limiting our ability to understand how archaeological sites function as active places within modern cultural landscapes. Heritage scholarship has challenged static definitions of archaeological sites as relics of a closed past, instead emphasising that sites acquire new layers of meaning through long-term processes of use, reuse, reinterpretation and engagement which extend well beyond their original periods of construction (Äikäs & Ahola, 2020: 174). From this perspective, contemporary practices, including informal ritual, commemoration, and personal acts of deposition, can be understood not as external disturbances but as integral components of the ongoing life histories of archaeological places.

Contemporary deposition also requires consideration beyond explicitly religious frameworks. Houlbrook (2015) notes that motivations for coin deposition vary and that participation need not imply shared belief. Houlbrook (2022) further challenges the dismissal of contemporary assemblages as “ritual litter”, arguing for recognition of their heritage value. These perspectives support consideration of spiritual, personal and mundane explanations for material deposited at heritage sites.

In Malta, prehistoric sites occupy a particularly prominent position within both national heritage narratives and popular understanding. The island’s Late Neolithic megalithic structures were early on, and continue to be, frequently associated, both academically and publicly, with ritual, fertility and cultic interpretations (Renfrew, 1986), despite scholarly caution regarding such frameworks (Stoddart, 2022: 6). Such early interpretations have contributed to the perception of these sites as spiritually charged places, encouraging visitors to engage with them in ways that extend beyond passive observation. Heritage Malta curators have encountered contemporary material suggestive of ritual or spiritual deposition at various prehistoric sites, including Ħaġar Qim, Mnajdra, and Skorba. This material comprises a range of objects, predominantly crystals of different shapes, colours and sizes. Although such objects may have spiritual significance, their presence alone cannot establish depositional intent. These observations derive from routine curatorial practice. Within this wider context, the Ħal Tarxien pit attracted attention because of the quantity and diversity of deposited material concentrated within a single feature. This qualitative assessment, informed by curatorial experience, prompted the systematic examination of the recovered assemblage presented here.

This paper examines contemporary depositional practices through the analysis of an assemblage recovered from a single feature within the Ħal Tarxien Prehistoric Complex. The focus of the study is a rock-cut pit originally identified in 1921, which was reopened in 2010 and remained open until 2024. Over this fourteen-year period, the pit accumulated a substantial quantity of modern material, including coins from across the globe, spiritual paraphernalia, personal objects, and items introduced unintentionally. Unlike many instances of modern deposition that are cleared sporadically and without record, the contents of this pit were systematically removed and documented, creating an assemblage derived from a single, clearly defined feature and deposited within a known, limited timeframe. Analysis of the recovered material explores how contemporary beliefs, personal narratives, and collective behaviours intersect with a prehistoric archaeological context. Rather than approaching contemporary deposits solely as conservation threats, the paper treats them as material evidence for ongoing processes of meaning-making and heritage engagement. In doing so, it contributes to broader debates on contemporary deposits, site biography, and heritage-making, while also addressing the practical challenges such practices pose for site management at one of Malta’s largest prehistoric complexes.

sec.title: Ħal Tarxien Prehistoric Complex
sec.p: The Ħal Tarxien Prehistoric Complex, Malta, comprises four megalithic structures dating to the Late Neolithic period, during the fourth and third millennia BC (Figure 1). Three principal apsidal buildings, known as the Southern, Central and Eastern buildings, stand alongside a smaller, heavily damaged Easternmost structure (Evans, 1971: 117-118). The complex was first excavated by Themistocles Zammit between 1915 and 1919, with supplementary investigations undertaken by Thomas Ashby in 1921 (Ashby, 1924). In 1992, it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

(B) Modelo digital de elevación de Malta que indica la ubicación del Complejo Prehistórico de Ħal Tarxien. (C) Plano del Complejo Prehistórico de Ħal Tarxien que muestra la posición del pozo.

sec.p: This study concerns a rock-cut pit situated in the north-east area of Room M within the Central building (Figure 1). The feature was uncovered during Ashby’s investigations in 1921. Beneath deposits of loose stones and burnt earth, he identified an opening approximately 41 cm in diameter, sealed by a circular stone slab. The opening led into a bell-shaped pit approximately 1.58 m deep and up to 1.3 m wide (Figure 2a). Ashby interpreted the feature as either a cistern or a granary (1924: 95-96).

A shallow basin associated with a natural fissure was also identified beside the pit. Its relationship with water informed subsequent interpretations of the feature. Zammit (1930: 26) described the pit as a cistern and recorded that its sealing slab was replaced following excavation, after which the feature was buried beneath stones and earth. Heritage Malta relocated and reopened it in 2010 (Grima, 2016: 38).

caption.title: (a) Dibujo en sección del pozo, reproducido de Grima (2016: 38), a partir de Ashby (1924); (b) el pozo en el momento de su redescubrimiento en 2010; (c) la depresión tal como se observó en 2024.
caption.p: (a) Section drawing of the pit, reproduced from Grima (2016: 38), after Ashby (1924); (b) the pit at the time of its rediscovery in 2010; (c) the depression as observed in 2024.

sec.p: Grima (2016: 38) subsequently supported a water-related interpretation, identifying the lateral depression as a catchment basin and noting that water could still collect there through the fissure. These interpretations concern the feature’s prehistoric function, which remains distinct from its contemporary use as a receptacle for visitor deposits.

Following its reopening in 2010, the pit remained open until 2024, accumulating coins and other modern objects. In January 2024, its condition was reassessed because of this accumulation and the associated conservation concerns. A decision was taken to remove, document and analyse the contents before resealing the pit with its original slab. The recovered material forms the assemblage examined in this paper.

sec.title: Methodology

p.italic: Removal of Modern Objects from the Pit

sec.p: Heritage Malta staff carried out the removal of the objects from the pit. The process involved descending into the pit using a ladder, collecting the materials by hand or with a trowel, and transferring them into a bucket which was subsequently emptied into large plastic crates. Over the course of two days, this process was repeated until the pit was fully cleared. After collection, the objects were dry sieved to remove any dust and placed in clean crates.

After the objects were collected, the sorting process commenced. The first step involved separating the coins from the other materials. Coins were manually sorted and placed in separate crates, while the other materials were photographed and analysed. Non-monetary objects were subsequently discarded. The objects were classified according to their interpreted mode of deposition. For the Ħal Tarxien assemblage, “deposits” is used descriptively, encompassing both deliberate placement and unintentional introduction. The term “offering” is reserved for possible devotional or spiritual interpretations, which remain provisional. Two principal categories were identified: ‘intentional’ and ‘unintentional’, reflecting whether objects were interpreted as having been purposefully placed within the pit or having entered inadvertently. Within the intentional category, a distinction was made between ‘meaningful’ and ‘collective behaviour’ depositions. Meaningful depositions denote material deliberately placed in the pit on account of its perceived significance, whether ‘spiritual’ or ‘personal’ in nature. Collective behaviour refers to possible influences of imitation or shared practices on intentional deposition. These influences may coexist with personal or spiritual meaning. All classifications are provisional interpretations of depositional processes and meanings, and an individual object may be compatible with more than one explanation. The unintentional category was subdivided into ‘human action’ and ‘external action’. Human action refers to material that entered the pit through human activity without deliberate intent, while external action designates objects introduced through non-human processes (e.g., wind action and animal activity). This classificatory framework is illustrated in Figure 3.

caption.title: Marco clasificatorio que ilustra los procesos de deposición interpretados identificados en el conjunto del pozo.
caption.p: Classificatory framework illustrating the interpreted depositional processes identified within the pit assemblage.

sec.p: The next step involved separating euro coins from non-euro coins, as the shared circulation of the euro across multiple countries limits their potential to indicate the geographical origin of the individuals who deposited them. Euro coins were sorted by denomination (e.g., 1c, 2c, 5c, 10c, 20c, 50c, €1, €2) and placed in labelled bags indicating their contents. The euro coins were subsequently returned to circulation and were not retained as part of the research collection. Non-euro coins were grouped together and stored in a separate container. The final step consisted of cleaning the coins using weak acid (vinegar) to better expose their surfaces, rinsing them with water to remove the acids and other residues, air-drying them and then placing them in a single plastic container. Following analysis, most non-euro coins were returned to circulation, while some heavily worn examples were retained by the curatorial team.

The non-euro coins were analysed to identify their issuing country or territory, currency name, denomination, metal type and condition. The issuing country was considered a potential indirect indicator of depositor origin, while recognising that it cannot conclusively establish an individual depositor’s nationality or place of residence. Each coin was examined individually, and the relevant data were recorded in an Excel spreadsheet. For geographical summaries, coins issued in Taiwan were grouped under China, giving 46 country categories across the assemblage. Currency values were calculated separately for each currency, with New Taiwan dollars therefore listed separately in Table 1. The total value of each currency was calculated by summing the face values of coins whose denominations were clearly identifiable. Values were first standardised into the primary unit of each national currency (e.g. cents to dollars, pence to pounds). Exchange values were calculated using the European Central Bank (ECB) euro foreign exchange reference rates for 31 December 2025. For currencies not included in the ECB dataset, supplementary publicly available exchange rate sources were used. This approach allowed the total value of each currency to be expressed in euros for comparative purposes. The metal composition of each coin was identified using relevant entries on Numista (https://en.numista.com/). Withdrawn currencies, including the Croatian kuna, French franc, Irish pound, Maltese lira and Cuban convertible peso, were excluded from euro conversion, as applying exchange rates for 31 December 2025 would be methodologically inappropriate. Attributes that could not be confidently determined, due to factors such as surface erosion, were recorded as missing.

A quantitative approach was employed to make a descriptive comparison, by country, between visitor numbers recorded during 2021–2024 and non-euro coins accumulated in the pit between 2010 and 2024. Visitor data for the Ħal Tarxien Prehistoric Complex were obtained from Heritage Malta records, which document the country of origin of all visitors who were willing to provide such information. The cumulative number of visitors from 2021 to 2024 was calculated for each country and presented alongside the corresponding total number of coins collected. To ensure analytical consistency, non-euro coins originating from former national currencies of countries using the euro in 2024 were excluded (for example, France). All remaining countries were retained, including those with minimal contributions, in order to preserve the dataset’s full geographic diversity. For visualisation, a dual-axis combination chart was employed: visitor totals were represented as vertical bars on the left-hand y-axis, while coin totals were plotted as a line on the right-hand y-axis. This representation was chosen to enable the simultaneous observation of absolute visitor figures and coin totals, thereby facilitating a descriptive assessment of geographical patterns in the two datasets.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A substantial quantity of euro coins was recovered, although detailed recording focused on the non-euro assemblage. Informal visual assessment during sorting suggested that coins of 1, 2, 5, 10 and 20 cents predominated, with 50-cent, €1 and €2 coins less frequently encountered. These observations provide a qualitative description, as no systematic denomination counts were recorded. A total of 941 non-euro coins were retrieved from the pit. The assemblage was heavily dominated by material from Europe, which accounted for 697 coins, representing the largest share of the assemblage. North America formed a much smaller secondary group with 101 coins, followed by Asia with 90 coins. The remaining continents were only marginally represented, with Oceania contributing 24 coins, Africa 12 coins, and South America just 6 coins. A further 11 coins from the assemblage were unidentifiable, making it impossible to determine their origin or value. The identified non-euro coins were grouped into 46 country categories across all currency-producing continents. While Russia and Turkey are regarded as transcontinental countries spanning both Europe and Asia, for the purposes of this analysis Russia was classified as European, whereas Turkey was considered Asian, following United Nations (1999) regional classifications.

Based on the conversion methodology outlined above, the calculated euro values (Table 1) show considerable variation. The highest converted values were recorded for coins from the United Kingdom (€37.70), Switzerland (€16.43), and Poland (€11.49). Moderate values were observed for coins from the United States (€6.60), the Czech Republic (€5.78), Norway (€4.01), Israel (€4.40), Bulgaria (€3.28), Australia (€2.93), and Hungary (€2.66). In contrast, coins from several countries contributed comparatively low converted values, often amounting to less than €0.50 per country (e.g. Bahrain, Chile, Thailand, Tunisia, and Trinidad and Tobago).

caption.title: Valor total de las monedas no euro recolectadas, convertidas a euros (€) utilizando los tipos de cambio del 31 de diciembre de 2025.
caption.p: Total value of collected non-euro coins, converted to euros (€) using exchange rates as of 31 December 2025.

sec.p: The condition of the identified non-euro coins spanned a full range of grades, from poor, deemed barely identifiable, to extremely fine, characterised by sharp and clear details with only slight wear on the design’s high points. Intermediate grades were also represented, indicating a broad spectrum of preservation states. The condition did not appear to be directly related to the metal composition, as all metal types exhibited coins in both lower and higher grades.

The geographical distributions of recorded visitors (T-Visitors, 2021-2024) and non-euro coins (T-Coins, 2010-2024) show strongly uneven patterns (Figure 4). Among the countries included in the comparison, Poland (5,742 visitors) and the United Kingdom (5,522 visitors) have the highest recorded visitor totals, followed by the United States of America (1,772 visitors) and Hungary (1,247 visitors). All remaining countries register fewer than 1,000 recorded visitors each. Coin totals are also highest for Poland (217), the United Kingdom (167) and the United States of America (85).

The distributions differ for some countries. Country-specific totals include Romania (58 coins; 839 recorded visitors), Switzerland (41 coins; 297 recorded visitors), Turkey (34 coins; 87 recorded visitors), Norway (31 coins; 43 recorded visitors) and South Africa (8 coins; 16 recorded visitors). Chile (1 coin; 548 recorded visitors) and China (3 coins; 512 recorded visitors) have small coin assemblages alongside larger recorded visitor totals. At the lower end of both distributions, numerous countries register fewer than 50 visitors and fewer than five coins. North Macedonia records two coins and one visitor.

These comparisons describe differences between the geographical distributions of the two datasets. Given the different recording periods, voluntary country-of-origin reporting and uncertainty about depositor origins, they cannot establish the proportion of visitors from each country who deposited coins. Possible explanations for variation in depositional engagement are considered in Section Discussion, Coins.

Se excluyen los países que utilizaban el euro en 2024. Los totales de visitantes se representan mediante barras en el eje y izquierdo y los totales de monedas mediante una línea en el eje y derecho.
caption.p: Comparison by country of recorded visitor totals (T-Visitors, 2021-2024) and non-euro coin totals (T-Coins, 2010-2024) at the Ħal Tarxien Prehistoric Complex. Countries using the euro in 2024 are excluded. Visitor totals are represented by bars on the left-hand y-axis and coin totals by a line on the right-hand y-axis.

sec.p: The non-coin assemblage recovered from the pit was provisionally classified according to possible modes of deposition, using the framework outlined in Figure 3. These assignments indicate plausible interpretations rather than established depositional histories. Items classified as ‘spiritual meaningful’ included six crystals, three glassy pebbles, a red pouch interpreted as a Chinese good luck charm, a small humanoid-like figurine, and a Virgin Mary pendant. A token from the Shrine of Mount Carmel was also recovered; however, its classification remains ambiguous, as it may represent either a spiritual meaningful or a personal meaningful deposition. An Alcoholics Anonymous coin was provisionally assigned to the ‘personal meaningful’ category. An unopened condom was considered in relation to possible personal meaning, although accidental loss or casual discard cannot be excluded. Three rings presented classificatory uncertainty and were therefore assigned to both the personal meaningful and human-action categories. Two lollipop sticks were considered under collective behaviour, although their presence alone does not establish imitation or shared motivation. Accidental loss or casual discard are also possible. Other items, including two plastic bottles, two plastic bottle caps, and a packet of chewing gum, were assigned to both the collective behaviour and human-action categories due to uncertainty surrounding their mode of deposition. Paper fragments (e.g., ticket pieces) and several plastic bags were assigned to three categories, collective behaviour, human action, and external action, reflecting continued ambiguity regarding their depositional pathways. Items provisionally assigned to the human-action category included a tallinja card (bus card), two pairs of sunglasses, wired headphones, a bear image, a broken headband, a button, a hair clip, a packet of tissues, prescription glasses, four keys, a broken cable tie, two earrings, string, safety pins, a toy axe, two pencils, and a crystal jewellery pendant. The classification of the bear image under human action is provisional, as its cartoon design suggests a children’s item that may have been lost accidentally. Deliberate deposition for personal or spiritual reasons cannot be excluded. The keys’ original function and mode of deposition remain uncertain. Their classification under human action is provisional, and deliberate placement cannot be excluded. Lastly, items assigned solely to the external-action category included a screw and nut, as well as animal bones, likely originating from a rodent. The assemblage also included a £5 Bank of England banknote, a Christmas tree sticker, a washer, a fabric fragment, a metal piece and miscellaneous small objects and fragments. The non-coin objects recovered from the pit are presented in Figure 5.

caption.title: Objetos recuperados del pozo del Complejo Prehistórico de Ħal Tarxien, excluidas las monedas. La fotografía se tomó inmediatamente después de la extracción del material del pozo.
caption.p: Non-coin objects recovered from the pit at the Ħal Tarxien Prehistoric Complex. The photograph was taken immediately after the material was removed from the pit.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The non-euro coin assemblage recovered from the pit at the Ħal Tarxien Prehistoric Complex provides material insight into contemporary visitor engagement with prehistoric places. The assemblage suggests repeated deliberate deposition, potentially influenced by international visitation, cultural expectations and the pit’s open condition. Deliberate coin deposition may encompass spiritual, personal and secular forms of engagement, and cannot be assigned a single meaning from the material evidence alone. The concentration of coins within a single open feature, combined with their cumulative deposition over time, closely parallels patterns documented at other sites (Houlbrook, 2015: 173). Comparative studies have shown that coins are among the most prevalent objects used in contemporary depositional practices, largely due to their widespread cultural acceptability and low material cost (Jonuks & Äikäs, 2019: 13). The results presented here support this interpretation. The generally low converted euro values are consistent with coin deposition as a relatively low-cost form of participation. The act of deposition may have held significance beyond monetary worth, although converted values alone cannot conclusively establish the motivations of individual depositors. Historically, the declining economic value of coins from the seventeenth century onwards facilitated their increasing use in symbolic and ritual contexts (Jonuks et al., 2010: 277). By the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, coin deposition had become firmly embedded within touristic behaviour, particularly at publicly accessible features such as wells and springs (Jonuks & Äikäs, 2019: 14). This historical trajectory is relevant to the Ħal Tarxien assemblage, as the pit may have been perceived by visitors as analogous to a well-like feature. Such a perception offers a plausible explanation for the disproportionately high concentration of coins within this feature compared to other areas of the site, although limited depositional activity was also identified elsewhere within the complex.

The geographic diversity of the assemblage further underscores the international character of engagement with the site. Coins grouped into 46 country categories, spanning all currency-producing continents, situate the Ħal Tarxien Prehistoric Complex within broader transnational networks of mobility and heritage consumption. This diversity aligns closely with Malta’s role as a major international tourism destination and provides material evidence for the global reach of the site. At the same time, the predominance of European-origin coins reflects Malta’s geographic proximity to mainland Europe and the composition of its primary visitor markets. The uneven correspondence between recorded visitor numbers and coin totals raises the possibility of variation in depositional engagement. Visitors may differ in whether they deposit coins, how many they leave and which currencies they select. Cultural expectations, personal meanings and responses to deposits already present in the pit are possible influences on these choices. Differences in everyday cash use between countries may also influence which coins visitors carry and have available for deposition. These interpretations remain provisional, given voluntary visitor reporting, the different periods covered by the datasets and the uncertain relationship between coin origin and depositor identity. The comparison nevertheless raises questions about how depositional practices vary among visitors and visitor groups, providing a basis for further investigation. The assemblage is compatible with visitors depositing coins already in their possession. However, the recorded condition may reflect alteration within the pit and subsequent cleaning as well as earlier wear. Neither condition nor the range of metal types establishes whether coins were selected specifically for deposition. Opportunistic use of available coins therefore remains a possible interpretation. Coin deposition may provide a simple and accessible means of engaging with a prehistoric place, potentially drawing on shared practices of leaving coins at particular locations. At Ħal Tarxien, the recovered material records repeated use of the pit as a depositional focus. This activity may represent an additional form of visitor engagement alongside formal interpretive frameworks. Through these deposits, visitors leave material traces of their presence and may contribute new meanings to the prehistoric landscape.

The study demonstrates that contemporary depositional practices, when systematically documented and analysed, can provide valuable insight into how heritage sites continue to be actively negotiated and reinterpreted in the present. Some limitations should nevertheless be acknowledged. Visitor country-of-origin data were collected on site from visitors who voluntarily supplied this information. Visitors who did not provide their country of origin are consequently absent from the country-specific totals, and the completeness of these records may vary between countries. The visitor records cover 2021-2024, whereas the coin assemblage accumulated between 2010 and 2024. As individual deposits cannot be dated, the coin totals cannot be restricted to the period covered by the visitor records. As a result, discrepancies between visitor counts and coin totals, such as instances where coin numbers exceed recorded visitor numbers (e.g. North Macedonia), may reflect recording limitations rather than depositional behaviour alone. In addition, the presence of non-euro coins cannot always be assumed to correspond directly to the nationality of the individuals who deposited them, as visitors may carry currency from countries other than their own. Nevertheless, countries with larger recorded visitor totals and coin assemblages offer a clearer descriptive basis for comparing the two distributions, while the different recording periods and uncertain depositor origins continue to limit interpretations of visitor engagement.

In the authors’ curatorial experience, local residents have not commonly been observed depositing objects at the site, although their participation cannot be excluded. Local involvement might reflect personal or collective attachments to the monuments, but this possibility cannot be evaluated from the assemblage alone. The issuing country of a non-euro coin does not establish its depositor’s place of residence, while euro coins may be deposited by both residents and overseas visitors. The available evidence consequently leaves the relative contributions of these groups unresolved.

Moving beyond the coin assemblage, the non-coin objects recovered from the pit suggest a broader range of possible depositional behaviours. While the placement of coins may, in part, reflect routinised or collectively learned practices (Banerjee, 1992), some non-coin objects may indicate more personalised forms of engagement. Deliberate deposition may also reflect secular tourist behaviour, including casual participation, imitation, play or the disposal of an item already being carried. These possibilities remain provisional because no visitor interviews were conducted. Accidental loss and environmental introduction must also be considered. Sunglasses, for example, may have fallen from visitors as they leaned over the barrier, while lightweight materials, including paper fragments, may have entered through wind action. Object type alone cannot conclusively establish whether deposition was intentional or what meaning it held.

Alongside these possible secular and unintentional processes, several objects invite consideration of spiritual or personal meanings. While the accumulation of coins and other material within the pit may have acted as an initial prompt, additional symbolic or personal factors are likely to have influenced decisions to deposit non-coin objects. Items interpreted as spiritually meaningful form a significant component of the assemblage. These included multiple crystals of varying sizes and hues, glassy pebbles, a red pouch, a small humanoid-like figurine, and a Christian medallion depicting the Virgin Mary. In contemporary esoteric contexts, crystals are associated with spiritual practices, where their material properties are interpreted as sources of energy (Teidearu, 2022: 218). Crystal use forms part of a broader range of contemporary spiritual practices, including New Spirituality (Teidearu, 2022: 213). Neo-paganism provides one relevant context for comparison (Leskovar, 2013), particularly in relation to engagements with prehistoric sites and iconography (Muscat, 2015: 188; Rountree, 2014: 91-93). While it is not possible to attribute these deposits to specific belief traditions, the presence of multiple crystals within a partially concealed, enclosed feature suggests that the pit may have been perceived by some visitors as a suitable locus for spiritually oriented acts. The Virgin Mary pendant and the token from the Shrine of Mount Carmel have recognisable devotional associations and may have been deposited as offerings. The crystals and red pouch also invite consideration of possible spiritual or protective meanings. These associations do not establish the intentions of individual depositors.

The interpretation of certain objects remains particularly complex. The deposition of an unopened condom, for example, may plausibly be accidental. However, it also invites consideration in light of persistent popular narratives surrounding Late Neolithic fertility cults. Scholarly debates concerning fertility symbolism in prehistoric Malta have a long history (Bonanno, 1986; Gimbutas, 1974; Veen, 1992), although such interpretations have consistently been treated with caution due to the difficulty of inferring belief systems from archaeological material (Renfrew, 1986; Stoddart, 2022). Nevertheless, these ideas have gained traction in popular discourse, and it is possible that contemporary visitors may interpret prehistoric sites through this lens. In this context, the condom may represent a symbolic act informed by modern perceptions of the site rather than evidence of intentional ritual practice. Other objects further demonstrate the diversity of belief systems brought into the site. A red pouch containing degraded paper fragments was interpreted as a Chinese good luck charm (Figure 5). Its presence raises questions concerning cultural translation and the possible reinterpretation of objects with ritual or protective associations within a prehistoric heritage setting. However, its place of manufacture and purchase history were not established, and the depositor’s understanding of the object remains unknown. Similarly, an anthropomorphic figurine wearing a bright red garment and a Catholic medallion depicting the Virgin Mary point to a range of spiritual and religious references coexisting within the assemblage. Together, these objects highlight the plurality of belief systems through which visitors may engage with the site and suggest that some individuals felt compelled to materially express these beliefs within the prehistoric setting.

Not all meaningful deposition, however, appears to have been spiritual in nature. Personal experience and emotional connection to the site may also have played a role. Malta’s prehistoric monuments occupy a prominent place in local cultural memory, frequently appearing on coinage, stamps, and in folklore (Mifsud-Chircop, 1994). In Malta, visits to prehistoric sites such as the Ħal Tarxien Prehistoric Complex have long formed part of childhood experience, particularly through school visits, and continue to play a role in the formation of young people’s relationships with these monuments. For many local visitors, early encounters with such sites are formative, fostering personal and emotional connections that extend beyond their archaeological significance. The recovery of an Alcoholics Anonymous sobriety coin provides a particularly striking example of deeply personal engagement. Sobriety coins mark significant milestones within the recovery process and may represent moments of considerable emotional and symbolic weight. As McVey (2016: 136) notes, participation in Alcoholics Anonymous often involves a spiritual reorientation centred on a God of one’s understanding, suggesting that the deposition of such an object may represent an act of reflection, commemoration, or symbolic transition. While the precise circumstances surrounding its deposition cannot be reconstructed, the presence of this item underscores the capacity of prehistoric sites to serve as settings for highly individualised meaning-making.

Taken together, the non-coin assemblage reveals the pit as a space where accidental loss, casual discard, spiritual expression, and deeply personal acts intersect. While these objects cannot be used to infer the original function or belief systems associated with the site, they nevertheless attest to its continued social relevance. As Finn (1997: 169) cautions, archaeological sites risk being framed as “culturally dead” when treated solely as static monuments, detached from ongoing engagement. The objects discussed here demonstrate that the Ħal Tarxien Prehistoric Complex continues to accrue new meanings through contemporary practices. These meanings do not necessarily reflect prehistoric realities but instead reveal how modern visitors negotiate identity, belief, memory, and experience within an ancient architectural setting.

The recovery and analysis of the pit assemblage demonstrate that contemporary deposits can be approached as both an interpretive resource and a management problem. Treating contemporary deposits as data rather than simply as refuse yields clear analytical benefits, yet it also exposes significant practical, ethical, and methodological challenges for heritage professionals working at heavily visited archaeological sites.
Benefits

A primary benefit of documenting contemporary deposits is that they provide material evidence for living relationships with heritage. The assemblage shows that visitors do not engage with the Ħal Tarxien Prehistoric Complex solely through formal interpretation (e.g., signage, guided narratives, museum framing), but also through acts that materialise belief, memory, and participation. In this sense, contemporary deposits contribute to the site’s ongoing biography, revealing how Late Neolithic architecture is continually re-authored through modern practices. Such evidence is easily lost through routine clearance, meaning that systematic recording produces an otherwise unavailable dataset for understanding how heritage functions as a social space.

A second benefit lies in the assemblage’s capacity to inform visitor studies. Patterns of deposition, including the dominance of low-value coins and the presence of culturally specific objects (e.g., pendants, tokens), suggest possible motivations and behavioural patterns. While deposits cannot be straightforwardly mapped onto visitor identity, the material nonetheless provides a complementary perspective to conventional visitor metrics by capturing acts that visitors choose to perform rather than merely their presence on site. This has practical value for communication strategies, as it identifies the forms of engagement that are most likely to recur and therefore the points at which interpretive messaging can be most effectively targeted.

Finally, the assemblage has benefits for collections practice and heritage decision-making. A documented, time-bounded deposit, from a single feature, such as the one analysed in this study, offers an opportunity to develop protocols for material classification and retention. By treating this material systematically, the project establishes a framework that can be applied elsewhere, supporting transparent and defensible decisions regarding what is retained, how it is recorded, and why it is ultimately discarded or potentially accessioned.
Challenges

Despite these benefits, the deposits create significant conservation and safety challenges. Accumulated material can trap moisture, promote corrosion, introduce salts and contaminants, abrade surfaces through repeated impact, and encourage further deposition by increasing the visibility of deposits within a feature. In enclosed or hard-to-access spaces such as this pit, continued deposition also generates risks associated with retrieval, including staff working in confined conditions and the potential for accidental damage during removal. The management burden is therefore not incidental but structural: once a feature becomes established as a depositional locus, it tends to attract repeated deposition.

The assemblage also raises ethical and interpretive tensions. While the study treats deposits as evidence for meaning-making, their removal may be perceived by some visitors as the rejection of personal or spiritual acts. This is particularly sensitive where objects have clear devotional associations or are linked to personal narratives (e.g., a token marking a recovery milestone). Heritage management must therefore negotiate a balance between respecting visitor motivation and maintaining the integrity of the site. There is a further tension between acknowledging contemporary ritualised practices and avoiding their inadvertent encouragement. Publicly foregrounding deposits as meaningful can legitimise deposition and increase its frequency, while ignoring them may reinforce the framing of such materials as “rubbish” and obscure the social dynamics that generate them.

A further challenge concerns classification uncertainty. As demonstrated by ambiguous items (e.g., rings, paper fragments, lightweight plastics), it is not always possible to distinguish intentional deposition from accidental loss, nor spiritual intent from casual action. Interpretations remain probabilistic, shaped by contextual cues (e.g., object type) rather than demonstrable intent. This constrains inference, in that the assemblage can speak clearly to the fact of deposition and to broad patterns, but only tentatively to individual motivations. Related to this are issues of representativeness. The dataset derives from one feature that functioned as an especially attractive depositional target, meaning it cannot be assumed to reflect site-wide behaviour in equal measure.

No interviews with site staff or visitors were conducted as part of this study. The contextual observations derive from routine curatorial experience and cannot establish the exact motivations of individual depositors. Future research combining staff and visitor interviews with direct observation could investigate the circumstances of contemporary deposition and the meanings attributed to these practices.

Finally, the study highlights challenges associated with documentation, retention, and disposal. Recording contemporary deposits requires time, staff capacity, and storage space, all of which are constrained in operational heritage settings. Decisions about what to retain must therefore remain proportionate and context-dependent. In this case, analytical value was generated through systematic documentation and analysis rather than long-term retention. While retaining all material is rarely feasible or desirable, discarding material without prior analysis risks the loss of valuable evidence for contemporary engagement.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This paper has demonstrated that contemporary deposits within the Ħal Tarxien Prehistoric Complex constitute more than incidental debris and should be understood as a material record of ongoing engagement with prehistoric space. The assemblage recovered from the rock-cut pit, accumulated over a defined fourteen-year period and derived from a single, clearly bounded feature, provides a rare opportunity to examine modern depositional practices within a Late Neolithic setting through systematic documentation and analysis. The results indicate that the pit functioned as a persistent focus for visitor deposition, dominated by coins but accompanied by a smaller and more heterogeneous range of objects that reflect both intentional acts and unintentional loss.

The coin assemblage documents repeated deposition involving currencies from a wide geographical range. The generally low converted euro values are consistent with coin deposition as a relatively low-cost form of participation. Opportunistic use of coins already in visitors’ possession remains a possible interpretation, but neither condition nor metal composition establishes how the coins were selected or the intentions behind their deposition. While coin quantities broadly corresponded with recorded visitor distributions, the differences observed raise the possibility of variation in depositional engagement, including potential cultural influences. This interpretation remains provisional given the different recording periods, voluntary visitor reporting and uncertainty about depositor origins. The assemblage cautions against treating coin totals as a direct proxy for visitor numbers, while providing an additional perspective on how visitors may engage with the site.

The non-coin assemblage further reveals the plurality of practices that converge within a single depositional locus. Several objects suggest spiritually oriented engagement, including crystals and devotional items, while others indicate more individualised or biographically significant acts. At the same time, the presence of potentially unintentional material underscores the interpretive limits of such assemblages. Depositional intent cannot always be inferred from object type alone. Nevertheless, even where motivations remain uncertain or debatable, the assemblage as a whole demonstrates that visitors continue to treat prehistoric spaces as settings for personal meaning-making.

The case study highlights the practical implications of contemporary deposits for conservation and site management. Accumulation within confined features can generate conservation risks and impose recurrent operational burdens, while decisions regarding documentation, retention, and disposal are constrained by resources and storage capacity. In the present case, analytical value was generated through recording and analysis prior to disposal, demonstrating that contemporary deposits can be treated as evidence without requiring long-term retention. More broadly, the assemblage suggests that routine clearance practices, when conducted without documentation, risk erasing valuable material traces of contemporary heritage engagement.
Ħal Tarxien, 27 October 2026
